youtube.title: Why Do Planes Fly at 35,000 Feet? (It's Not Speed) #science #facts #didyouknow
youtube.description:
Every airliner climbs to around 35,000 feet and stays there, higher than Mount Everest, in air you couldn't breathe. Climbing burns fuel, so why go so high? And why do eastbound and westbound flights use different heights?

From thin air and freezing jet engines to the weather ceiling, the pilots' 'coffin corner', and the 1956 Grand Canyon collision that rewrote the rules of the sky: this is the hidden why behind cruising altitude.

instagram.caption:
Planes fly at 35,000 feet to save fuel, not to go faster. ✈️

The air up there is about a third as thick, so there's far less drag, the cold makes jet engines more efficient, and most weather sits below. And eastbound flights use odd thousands of feet while westbound use even ones, a rule born from a 1956 tragedy.

Full story on our YouTube channel.

facts: Typical airliner cruise 31,000-42,000 ft (FAA AIM / industry)
Air density at 35,000 ft ~0.38 kg/m3 vs 1.225 at sea level (~31%) (NASA GRC standard atmosphere)
Tropopause ~36,000 ft at mid-latitudes; nearly all weather in the troposphere (NWS)
Coffin corner: stall speed meets critical Mach near the service ceiling (FAA handbook)
Step climbs as fuel burns off (airline practice)
30 June 1956 Grand Canyon collision, TWA 2 + United 718, 128 killed; led to the Federal Aviation Act 1958 and the FAA (Britannica)
US IFR hemispheric rule: magnetic course 0-179 odd thousands, 180-359 even thousands (FAA AIM 91.179)
